passage: The third time that week was in the hostel dining hall. Raghav, new in Vidya's house, passed her the dal and asked, "So where are you actually from? Like, really?" "Here. This city. I was born two streets from the school." "No, but originally?" Vidya smiled the smile she had practised. That morning a substitute teacher had told her, "Your English is so good," as if it were a surprise. On Monday the librarian had asked whether she'd "come on the scholarship". Taken one at a time, none of it was anything. Raghav wasn't being unkind; he looked honestly curious. But Vidya ate the rest of her dinner in silence, feeling like a visitor in the only place she had ever lived.

qa.q: Where was Vidya born?
qa.a: Two streets from the school, in this city.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling as she ate the rest of her dinner in silence?
qa.a: She felt out of place and alone, like a visitor in the only place she had ever lived, because Raghav's question was the third remark like it that week.

qa.q: What could Vidya choose to say the next time someone asks "originally?"
qa.a: She could calmly repeat that she is from here, or ask what makes them wonder, so she isn't swallowing it every time.

qa.q: How might Raghav see his question, compared with how it landed for Vidya?
qa.a: Raghav likely thought he was being friendly and curious, without knowing it was the third remark like that for her in one week.

grounding: A teenager hears repeated small remarks about where she is really from and how good her English is, and the build-up makes her feel like an outsider.

passage:
Dear Farhan,
City school, month two. The building has lifts! But I want to tell you the other thing.
On day one, a boy asked if we had electricity "back there". Last week Ma'am read my essay aloud and said, "Very good, especially for someone from a village school." Everyone clapped. Today in the lab a girl said, "You speak English so well, where did you learn?" I said, "In school, like you." She looked surprised.
None of them is cruel. I know that. But I keep counting them, like pebbles in my shoe. By evening my feet hurt from pebbles I can't show anyone.
Did anyone say things like this to you when you moved for college?
Tell your mother the essay was about her mango tree. Write soon.
Ganga

qa.q: What did Ma'am say after reading Ganga's essay aloud?
qa.a: "Very good, especially for someone from a village school."

qa.q: What does Ganga mean by "pebbles in my shoe"?
qa.a: Ganga feels each remark is tiny, but they keep piling up and hurting in a way that's hard to show anyone.

qa.q: What choice could Ganga make with these pebbles, rather than carrying them alone?
qa.a: Ganga could keep writing to Farhan, or tell a trusted teacher how the "especially for" comments feel, so the weight is shared.

qa.q: How might the girl in the lab have felt when Ganga said "In school, like you"?
qa.a: She may have been surprised, and perhaps briefly noticed that her question assumed something about Ganga.

grounding: A teenager new to a city school describes small, repeated remarks about a village background and English, adding up to feeling like an outsider.

passage: You want to know why I stopped answering in class, Sarita? It's not one big thing. It's small ones. My father sells vegetables near the station; everybody knows because he waves at the school bus. So when I topped the maths test, the teacher said, "Wah, a sabziwala's son, first!" Everyone laughed; he meant it as praise. Then the new coach asked if I'd need help with the fees before I'd even said anything. Then someone's mother at the parents' meeting said, "You speak so nicely!" like it was a trick. Each time I smile. Each time it's small. But by the end of the month I feel like I'm always being introduced as a surprise. Me, Vijay, a surprise. So today, after class, I finally told Ms Kurian, our class teacher. She listened, said it shouldn't be a joke, and she's talking to the maths teacher this week.

qa.q: What does Vijay's father do?
qa.a: He sells vegetables near the station.

qa.q: Why did Vijay stop putting his hand up in class?
qa.a: He was tired of being treated as a surprise; the small remarks piled up until speaking in class felt like inviting another one.

qa.q: What made telling Ms Kurian a good turning point?
qa.a: Vijay no longer carried it alone, and an adult who could act, by talking to the maths teacher, now knew about the pattern.

qa.q: How might the maths teacher see the "sabziwala's son" comment, and what could change after Ms Kurian talks to him?
qa.a: He likely thought it was praise; hearing how it landed might help him see that it marked Vijay out as an exception.

grounding: A teenager describes being repeatedly praised as surprisingly bright for his family background, small comments that add up to feeling singled out.

passage: I'm Sachin, and I sit behind Amandeep in our Year 10 form group in Leicester. I started keeping count after the careers fair. A visitor at the engineering stall shook his hand and asked, "And where are you really from?" Amandeep said, "Here. Born at the hospital down the road." The man laughed and waited, as if a better answer was coming. On Tuesday the new drama teacher told him his English was "lovely, so clear". He has never spoken anything else at school. On Thursday a supply teacher handed back his chemistry test, looked at the mark, then at him, and said, "Well! Didn't expect that." Each time, Amandeep smiled and gave a small nod. But on Friday, when our group was planning where to go after exams, he said, "Somewhere nobody asks where I'm from." Nobody laughed. I can't say what he felt exactly. I know he has stopped putting his hand up.

qa.q: Where was Amandeep first asked where he was really from?
qa.a: At the engineering stall at the careers fair.

qa.q: What does Amandeep's line about going "somewhere nobody asks where I'm from" suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests the small comments had piled up until he felt like an outsider in the town he was born in; Sachin noticed it didn't sound like a joke.

qa.q: After Friday, what choice does Sachin face, and what could make a difference?
qa.a: Sachin can keep counting silently or act on it, for example by checking in with Amandeep privately and, next time someone presses, backing up the first answer: "He said here."

qa.q: How might the visitor at the stall have seen the question, compared with how it landed?
qa.a: The visitor probably thought it was friendly curiosity, but by laughing and waiting for a 'better' answer, the man treated Amandeep's real home as not good enough.

grounding: A teenager born in the city is asked where he is really from, praised for his English and called surprisingly clever, and the small remarks add up to feeling like an outsider.

passage:
Monday, first week. Jaya had joined the private school in Class 11 on a scholarship. In the physics lab a boy leaned over her neat circuit and said, "Wow. Smart for a scholarship kid." Jaya laughed along. Her lab partner, Mehak, frowned but said nothing.
Two weeks later. The class teacher handed back the essays and smiled at Jaya. "Your English is really good, considering." Considering what, Jaya wanted to ask. At lunch a girl asked how she "managed" such marks "coming from there". Each thing was tiny. Jaya began eating her rotis in the library.
A month later. Mehak found her between the shelves. "You've stopped sitting with us." Jaya shrugged, then it came out. "Every day someone reminds me I'm the one who doesn't fit. Nobody means it. It's just every day." Mehak sat on the floor beside her and opened her tiffin. "Then tell me the next one when it happens. I'm listening."

qa.q: Where did Jaya start eating lunch?
qa.a: In the library, between the shelves.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when she said, "Nobody means it. It's just every day"?
qa.a: She felt worn down and singled out; no single comment was big, but the steady repetition made her feel she didn't belong at the new school.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the third beat, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Mehak came looking for Jaya and asked why she had stopped sitting with them, which let Jaya say the pattern out loud instead of carrying it alone.

qa.q: How might the class teacher have meant "really good, considering", and how did it land for Jaya?
qa.a: The teacher probably meant it as warm praise, but for Jaya the word 'considering' was one more sign that people expected less of her.

grounding: A scholarship student hears one small remark after another about being clever or well-spoken for her background, and over weeks they add up to feeling like an outsider.
